summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat, enacted in 2014, has been enforced since 23 October 2015. Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months (eight years) imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. The provisions are applied to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, so a trans traveller's exposure does not turn on religion or residency. Because the tests are birth sex and presentation, a trans visitor's documents, appearance or choice of partner can be policed as same-sex conduct.

Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. An Islamic court in Banda Aceh applied the 2014 provisions for the first time on 23 May 2017, caning two men 82 lashes each in front of hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in the same year two gay men aged 20 and 23 were sentenced to public caning.

Transgender residents have been targeted directly. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate January 2018 parlour raid in Aceh, police shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, paraded them in the street and forced them to shout "to become men"; the account describes torture of detainees.

The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, following an April arrest in which police broke into a toilet, and CBS News reported on 26 August 2025 that two men were publicly caned after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later instance is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
Aceh's treatment sits within a national pattern of official hostility toward LGBTQ people, but the province is the only sub-national unit in Indonesia with its own sexual-conduct offences, so its exposure is materially higher than in other provinces.

Regional scholarship engages the question directly: "The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement", by UIN Ar-Raniry scholars in QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405), analyses the rise of waria cases in the provincial capital through a sharia-law-enforcement lens, with keywords covering law enforcement, waria, Aceh, Islamic law and the Qanun. The inventory does not report the article's findings.

The UNSW Human Rights Research Centre report on violence against transgender women in Indonesia, which records the January 2018 detention of twelve trans women, is scoped Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific; the Aceh incidents above are drawn from separate Aceh reporting.
localsOnly:
Transgender Acehnese residents live under a code that defines offences by sex at birth, so local waria face exposure that does not apply to them in most other Indonesian provinces. The January 2018 North Aceh operation closed beauty salons, a documented livelihood for waria in the province, and paired arrest with forced haircutting and compelled male clothing.

The provincial scholarship cited above treats the number of waria in Banda Aceh as a law-enforcement question, indicating that local transgender residents are an object of sharia enforcement rather than a protected category under the Qanun.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not document how Aceh authorities treat a foreign identity document carrying an X marker or a marker that differs from the holder's presentation, and no case in this inventory involves a foreign visitor charged under Articles 63 or 64.

Unresolved: the inventory gives no Aceh-specific figure for violence against transgender residents and no per-capita comparison, so the scale of trans-directed harm in the province relative to general crime levels cannot be established here.

Unresolved: whether the 11 August 2025 sentencing and the caning reported by CBS News on 26 August 2025 are the same event is not stated by the sources.

Unresolved: no documented instance of sharia enforcement against trans people in Aceh later than August 2025 appears in this inventory; the absence of a later record is not evidence of a change in practice.
